story_text.value:
pi-cowboy is an agent orchestrator for Pi(https://pi.dev) and Herdr(https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr). Break large jobs into focused subtasks, hand them off to background agents running in parallel, and consolidate the results when they finish. Each agent runs in an isolated copy-on-write Git work-tree, minimising disk overhead.

pi-cowboy can orchestrate foreign harnesses too, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and more.

Feature highlights:

- Foreign harnesses: pi-cowboy agents can run in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pig and Pi-Bolt, as well as Pi. This gives you great flexibility in choosing how to spend your tokens. Running out of Codex usage? Switch your pi-cowboy harness to OpenCode, select one of its free models, and let it handle the rest. Pig and Pi-Bolt are pi variants that are more efficient, with a lower memory footprint and faster performance than pi. Because pi-cowboy is designed to run multiple agents in parallel, having a lower per-agent footprint is crucial. It prevents your machine from running out of resources and lets you have higher concurrency without choking your system.

- Concurrency limits: You can configure concurrency limits at every level. Running a local model with limited resources? If a simple task already takes hours to complete, the last thing you want is to overload your machine by running too many of them at once. Set concurrency limits for that model specifically to keep resource usage under control.

You can install it on Pi as a package:

  pi install npm:pi-cowboy #(requires `herdr` 0.8+)

story_text.value:
Hi everyone,

This started as an exploration into harnesses and locally hostable LLMs (the kind that uses less power than a small electric heater), and I used it as an opportunity to retool. I've tried popular ones like Cline, Claude Code, and Pi, but wanted a different UX and integrated sandboxes.

The solution that I've landed on is a responsive web interface where I can quickly drive progress. It feels like a microcosm of my day job: define and delegate tasks, organize using kanban, then review deliverables. And it also feels like the time I used to spend coding is now spent in code review with the agent, so I tried to optimize the UX to make review feel nicer.

One of my (maybe a bit niche) benchmark use-cases is how pleasant it is to make progress on hobby software projects while also out on a hike. This meant specifying low bandwidth usage and offline mode.

Now I can jot down an idea, start the task, and at some point down the trail: get a notification* that either clarification is needed, a decision needs to be made, or the code is ready for review. I've been having a good time with this.

To build MIKE, I exclusively used locally hostable LLMs (from Google, Meta, Qwen, Poolside, and DeepSeek) hosted with llama.cpp on my machines at home (Strix Halo and a 5090) to "compile" the code. The experience has gotten substantially better ever since DeepSeek’s release in July. Side note: I have a soft spot for llama.cpp since it was one of the first that made it possible to run this new tech at home, and its maintainers accepted a tiny improvement I made to error reporting. Oh the joys of having a PR get approved.

I plan on maintaining this, at least until similar features are supported by better tools. Until then, hope you find this useful!

5 minute demo: https://youtu.be/jexzLkZ50FU

p.s.

I didn't mention details about the sandbox earlier since most people seem to find this a bit boring. It was one of my critical requirements, and I opted to use an existing battle-tested sandbox. I'm not an expert on how the Linux kernel works, but seeing all the VM escape exploits recently is a bit scary, and I liked gVisor’s approach to the problem.

I'm also using Git worktrees to provision the agent’s workspace, as well as a read-only repository mount to provide relevant context when the agent looks for it.

*off by default

story_text.value:
My kids love their Yotos and I love Audiobookshelf. I wanted something in between that works as they get older and more control. I had two old Gen 2 players lying around that Yoto no longer supports.

It turns the player into an Audiobookshelf client. You browse your library with the two knobs, the 16x16 screen shows tiny cover art, and favourites and downloads sync back to the server. Its still keeps the NFC card concept, but they're optional: you can link books/favourites to any NFC card. It all runs locally, with no Yoto account or cloud.

It does require opening the player and soldering some wires to flash the initial firmware, but then its OTA after that.

Disclaimer: Its all Claude Code, Its an idea I've been slowly tinkering around in my spare time and never got very far so. I threw Claude Code at it and I was amazed at how well it did. Flashing, reading logs and fixing things - leaving me to just perform physical button presses and checks.

story_text.value: I compared 6 MCP proxies inside Claude Code. Most advertise 85–99% token savings, but those numbers assume every tool schema is loaded upfront, and Claude Code already avoids that. On real tasks, 4 of them used more tokens than no proxy at all, and 2 couldn't finish the tasks. So I built my own router, which cut tokens by 13–44% and completed every task.

story_text.value:
Self-hosting instructions in the README.

Hosted version: https://coastmath.com/

iOS app: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6809539979

This post is partially inspired by this thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50048344

``` > Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt.

>> No, they can't, at least not any semblance of quality. The cases we're seeing where this does kinda work is in ports and translation where all the rules are already documented in the best specification language possible with a way for the LLM to verify itself: code. We saw this close to a year ago now with Cloudflare and NextJS ```

This post mostly outlines how I am personally building with agents, as I am almost entirely hands-off.

Desired feature-set determined by having agents research existing products and feedback / feature requests on FIRE subreddits.

Features built using Opus 5.5 (xhigh) / Fable 5.1 (med/high) as orchestrator and Opus-5-5 low/medium as worker subagents.

Quality is attempted by running Opus-5-5 agents in a perpetual audit + fixer loop on the calculation / compliance engine until no medium+ severity can be found. The origin of each rule / logic must be backed up and documented in the codebase with a source.

Sonnet subagents run UX / QA audit on iOS simulators within the Claude Code desktop app, and Opus agents resolve all medium+ sev issues; also run on a perpetual loop.

I have not manually tested or used the app(s) for more than 30 minutes. For UX quality, agents' screenshots + associated context are fed to a combination of GPT / Gemini / Claude agents until consensus is achieved on quality (7/10+).

Early feedback from beta testers report extremely close results to Boldin / Projection Lab. There is also a feature to import your data from Boldin and Projection Lab into CoastMath if you wish to compare the results yourself.

There is also a SimpleFIN integration, if you wish to pull in your own transaction data and see how your financial future changes based on your monthly spending habits (e.g. when I will get to retire if I spend like I did in June vs. July?).

I'm sure there are other features I don't yet know about. Again, I've barely used the app.

Anyway, feel free to use / roast / steal. I don't think that any moat can exist in this class of products in the future (where the rules are laws that are visible to everyone) and I don't expect to turn a profit.

Estimated cost: maybe $2000 if done over the API? I did most of this using the $200 Max subscription.

title.value: Show HN: CoastMath: (Open Source) Personal Finance and Retirement Planner

story_text.value:
Sill (discussed here: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50112739) streams one Mac window, or the whole Desktop, to an iPhone or iPad and lets you control it by touch. It's open source, so I made an Android client for it. It's unofficial and not affiliated with Sill's author: it speaks Sill's existing protocol, so the Mac side is the stock Sill app, unchanged.

Install Sill on the Mac, sideload the APK from Releases onto an Android 11+ phone on the same Wi-Fi, tap your Mac in the list that shows on your phone, then look for the 12-digit code in Sill on your Mac, and type it into the Android app.

Then: tap to click, drag to scroll, hold-and-drag to select text or move windows, pinch to zoom the picture on the phone, a Draw toggle for whiteboard apps like tldraw, and a key row with Esc, Tab, Cmd/Ctrl/Option/Shift and arrows. It also works over Tailscale with Sill's Remote Access.

All of the code was written by Claude Code, working from Sill's Swift source and its Python test client; I tested it on a Pixel 9 Pro XL.

Not done yet: drawing the Mac's pointer, a trackpad mode, clipboard sync, and a Play Store listing (I don't have Play developer account, and new individual Play developer accounts can't publish their first app until they've tested an app with a closed test with 12 testers.)

(There's also a separate Android client in draft PR #89 on Sill's repo. This one is a standalone app with an installable APK. I should have checked the issues/PRs before I asked Claude to build this...)
